title: Cafeteria & Restaurant Workers Union, Local 473, AFL-CIO v. McElroy
lead: A satisfactory cafeteria cook lost her military-installation badge for undisclosed security reasons. The Court found explicit exclusion authority and no hearing requirement on this record, while four dissenters questioned how arbitrary grounds could ever be exposed without a chance to answer.

actors.name: Rachel Brawner
actors.role: Private restaurant employee excluded from the Naval Gun Factory cafeteria where she had worked more than six years.

actors.name: M & M Restaurants, Inc.
actors.role: Concessionaire employing Brawner; offered another restaurant position after exclusion.

actors.name: Rear Admiral Tyree and Lieutenant Commander Williams
actors.role: Commanding Superintendent and Security Officer who approved and implemented badge withdrawal.

actors.name: Secretary of Defense
actors.role: Defendant with the command officials in the access-restoration suit.

proceedings: District court granted officials summary judgment and dismissed.
Divided D.C. Circuit panel initially reversed, but that opinion was withdrawn; en banc court affirmed with four dissenters.
limits: Brawner was a concessionaire employee, not a discharged federal civil servant. No disloyalty or intentional misconduct charge was established, and the actual undisclosed ground remained unknown. The judgment does not approve arbitrary discrimination or establish every military-access procedure.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Brawner works inside a guarded ordnance installation
sections.cue: Why did her private job depend on a government badge?
paragraphs: Rachel Brawner worked more than six years as a short-order cook for M & M Restaurants, Inc., which considered her performance entirely satisfactory. Its cafeteria operated by concession inside Washington’s federally owned Naval Gun Factory. The installation designed, produced, and inspected naval ordnance, including highly classified systems. Guards controlled entry, and the Security Officer issued authorized-person identification badges under commanding Superintendent Rear Admiral Tyree.

The concession prohibited employment of anyone failing installation security or other regulatory requirements as determined by the Security Officer. Brawner remained a private employee; the federal government controlled the access necessary for this particular cafeteria job.

sections.title: The security officer takes her badge without explaining the concern
sections.cue: What happened when the employer and union sought discussion?
paragraphs: On November 15, 1956, Lieutenant Commander Williams required Brawner to return her badge because she failed installation security requirements. Tyree approved and cited the concession provision. At the request of her union, Cafeteria & Restaurant Workers Union, Local 473, AFL-CIO, M & M sought a meeting, but Tyree said it would serve no useful purpose. Brawner remained excluded and unable to work at that cafeteria.

M & M offered employment at another suburban Washington restaurant; Brawner declined because the location was inconvenient. The underlying security concern was never disclosed. The later majority emphasized that no one had charged disloyalty or intentional wrongdoing. It mentioned carelessness with a badge as something security requirements might encompass, not as a finding of what Brawner had done.

sources.pinpoint: Badge withdrawal and record limits; 367 U.S. at 888, 898–99

sections.title: The access-restoration suit reaches a constitutional question Greene reserved
sections.cue: Which appellate ruling was actually under review?
paragraphs: Brawner and her union sued the Defense Secretary, Superintendent, and Security Officer personally and officially, seeking among other relief restoration of badge and access. The district court granted officials summary judgment and dismissed. A divided appellate panel initially reversed, but its opinion was withdrawn on rehearing. The en banc D.C. Circuit affirmed with four dissenters.

The Supreme Court granted review because of a claimed conflict with Greene v. McElroy. Greene had invalidated a clearance procedure impairing an engineer’s profession without confrontation because explicit presidential or congressional authorization was missing; it had not finally decided constitutionality.

Justice Stewart applied the explicit-authorization requirement here, putting aside the government’s proposed lesser delegation standard for these different facts. If authorization existed, the Court would then address the due-process question Greene had reserved.

sources.pinpoint: Proceedings and Greene comparison; 367 U.S. at 888–90 & n.2

sections.title: Presidentially approved Navy regulations authorize command control of entry
sections.cue: Why did the majority find what Greene lacked?
paragraphs: Congress’s military and property powers and the President’s commander-in-chief role supported control over military premises. Congress entrusted naval property administration and custody to the Navy Secretary, permitted appropriate regulations, and required presidential approval of Navy Regulations. President Truman expressly approved the relevant regulations August 9, 1948.

Article 0701 matched command authority to command responsibility, subject to law and regulations. Article 0734 specifically excluded tradesmen and agents unless a commander authorized public business, requested private business, or needed services and supplies. The Court placed Brawner’s concession employment within that category and read it against the longstanding practice of command control over private entry.

The explicit regulation, not the concession alone, supplied authority. References to broad or absolute withdrawal power concerned that delegation and did not end constitutional analysis; the majority separately considered how lawful authority could be exercised.

sections.title: Stewart evaluates the function and the particular private interest
sections.cue: Why did the Court reject a categorical privilege shortcut yet deny a hearing?
paragraphs: Stewart rejected the simple claim that absence of a constitutional right to enter meant no protected interest could be affected. Due process does not invariably demand a trial-like hearing, but depends on the precise governmental function and private interest.

The majority understood this interest as work at one isolated installation, not ability to practice an entire trade. Brawner could cook for M & M elsewhere or another employer. Government acted as military proprietor managing internal affairs, rather than licensing a profession or regulating an entire industry. That distinguished broad occupational exclusions and supported analogy to historical control over governmental employment arrangements.

The majority acknowledged that government lacks an ordinary private employer’s complete freedom, citing United Public Workers and Wieman for constitutional constraints. It assumed openly arbitrary exclusion for being a Democrat or Methodist would be unconstitutional. Yet a rational stated security ground consistent with the concession did not, in its view, require charges and a hearing for each access withdrawal.

The record showed no established mark of disloyalty or infamy barring other work, and government counsel represented that this loss would not factually or legally preclude other federal-property employment. The Court did not decide Brawner’s character or actual undisclosed conduct. It held only that this limited exclusion, with traditional military-proprietary authority and the shown consequences, did not require the demanded procedure.

sources.pinpoint: Contextual due process; 367 U.S. at 894–99 & nn.8–10

sections.title: Brennan asks how forbidden grounds could be uncovered
sections.cue: What minimum process did the dissent seek?
paragraphs: Justice Brennan, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justices Black and Douglas, had serious authorization doubts but assumed the majority’s answer to focus on due process. The majority recognized protection against some arbitrary injuries; an unexplained security assertion could conceal exactly those grounds. Without inquiry, protection would exist only when an official volunteered an improper reason.

Brennan did not demand a full trial, confrontation, cross-examination, or proof beyond reasonable doubt. He sought some account of the alleged conduct and a chance to respond, so false charges or caprice could be exposed. A substantive right against arbitrariness without any procedural means to test it seemed contradictory.

He also disputed the majority’s reassuring account of stigma. In contemporary understanding, security-risk language suggested communism or disloyalty, not merely harmless talkativeness. Even if sound reasons existed, government should not impose such a potentially infamous designation and destroy a valuable relationship without explanation and response. He did not find Brawner disloyal or establish that the decision necessarily lacked cause.

sections.title: The denial of relief is affirmed on the record’s limited characterization
sections.cue: Which account of the case would overstate it?
paragraphs: On June 19, 1961, the Court affirmed, five to four, leaving denial of badge-restoration relief intact. It independently sustained explicit command authority and the procedure used in these circumstances.

Calling this simply dismissal from federal employment for disloyalty would misdescribe both job and record. Brawner was privately employed, and the majority identified failure of installation security requirements without a charge of disloyalty or deliberate wrongdoing. The decision rejected a categorical right/privilege shortcut while denying this hearing claim. It supplies no later employment history or present-day military-access rule beyond its historical holding.

sources.pinpoint: Judgment and assigned correction; 367 U.S. at 894–99, 902
